title: Nausea and yellow vision on digoxin — recognise, investigate and act safely

blocks.text: Nausea and yellow vision on digoxin — recognise, investigate and act safely

AMaC MRCP PACES23 | Round 5 | R5-235 | Station 2: acute consultation | 20 minutes | Communication, clinical judgement and patient welfare (C, E, F, G) | AMaC educational scoring, not official PACES marks

A 79-year-old with atrial fibrillation and chronic kidney disease reports nausea, poor appetite, yellow-tinged vision and dizziness. Take a focused history, determine urgency and explain your plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: Hook: Suspected digoxin toxicity, potentially with bradyarrhythmia or ventricular arrhythmia. Serum concentration can be misleading if sampled soon after a dose or considered without the clinical context. Trap: The decision to use DigiFab follows severity and expert toxicology guidance, not simply the presence of visual disturbance.

rows: “First, I want to check how unwell you are.”
Assess stability and the specific emergency signs.
“I’ll ask questions that help us distinguish the causes.”
Ask digoxin dose and timing, renal deterioration, dehydration, interacting drugs (including amiodarone and some antibiotics), vomiting and syncope; check observations, pulse and ECG.
“I will arrange tests and support appropriate to the risk.”

Stop digoxin temporarily, urgently check ECG, electrolytes especially potassium and magnesium, renal function and a correctly timed serum digoxin level; correct relevant disturbances with specialist advice.
“I will explain when we must act urgently.”

Life-threatening arrhythmia, cardiac arrest or severe hyperkalaemia requires emergency toxicology/cardiology assessment for digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab). Do not delay resuscitation awaiting digoxin concentration.
Dismisses nausea and yellow vision as unrelated
Recognises possible digoxin toxicity, especially with renal impairment or medication changes
Asks about bradycardia, syncope and life-threatening arrhythmia symptoms
Waits for routine outpatient bloods despite collapse
Checks pulse, BP, consciousness and urgent 12-lead ECG; arranges monitored assessment
Activates urgent resuscitation response for dysrhythmia or instability
Withholds digoxin while evaluating toxicity, dose and recent interacting medicines
Checks diuretic use, dehydration, renal decline and recent digoxin exposure
Uses a single normal digoxin level to exclude toxicity
Checks U&E, potassium, magnesium, renal function and appropriately timed serum digoxin level
Interprets level by sampling time and clinical/ECG findings, not threshold alone
Seeks urgent medical/toxicology review, corrects electrolytes cautiously and monitors rhythm
Discusses digoxin-specific antibody fragments for life-threatening toxicity with specialists
Reassures that yellow vision is harmless
Explains possible drug toxicity and need for urgent monitored assessment
Provides a clear medicine reconciliation and follow-up plan after stabilisation

blocks.text: Patient is concerned about the symptoms and asks: ““Why is my vision yellow?”” The role-player provides symptoms from the brief and relevant positive/negative history only when asked; avoid volunteering the diagnosis. Respond to clear empathetic explanations.
Q1. What clues point to toxicity? — Nausea, yellow/green visual change, bradyarrhythmia or other dysrhythmia on digoxin.
Q2. Can a therapeutic level exclude it? — No; timing and clinical context including potassium and ECG determine interpretation.
Q3. What immediate actions? — Withhold digoxin and assess ABC, ECG, haemodynamics, renal function and electrolytes.
Q4. What makes this life-threatening? — Haemodynamic compromise, severe arrhythmia or serious electrolyte disturbance.
Q5. What is antidotal escalation? — Discuss digoxin-specific antibody fragments with toxicology for life-threatening toxicity.

THINK: Suspected digoxin toxicity, potentially with bradyarrhythmia or ventricular arrhythmia. Serum concentration can be misleading if sampled soon after a dose or considered without the clinical context. SAY: avoid certainty without confirmation. DO: Stop digoxin temporarily, urgently check ECG, electrolytes especially potassium and magnesium, renal function and a correctly timed serum digoxin level; correct relevant disturbances with specialist advice. NUMBERS: 20-minute encounter. TRAP: The decision to use DigiFab follows severity and expert toxicology guidance, not simply the presence of visual disturbance. FINISH: Life-threatening arrhythmia, cardiac arrest or severe hyperkalaemia requires emergency toxicology/cardiology assessment for digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab). Do not delay resuscitation awaiting digoxin concentration.
